title: Intel Smashes Earnings Estimates as AI Boom Drives Strongest Growth in 15 Years
excerpt: The chipmaker posted 25% revenue growth to $16.1 billion in Q2, raised its capital spending plans to over $20 billion, and forecast Q3 results well above Wall Street expectations.
body:
• Intel reported Q2 2026 revenue of $16.1 billion, up 25% year-over-year, with adjusted earnings of $0.42 per share — nearly double the $0.22 analysts expected.
  • Data center and AI segment revenue surged 59% to $6.3 billion, driven by soaring demand for CPUs used in agentic AI workloads.
  • The company raised its 2026 capital expenditure forecast from $18 billion to over $20 billion to meet demand that CEO Lip-Bu Tan says is "outpacing supply."
  • Intel guided Q3 revenue of $15.8–$16.8 billion and adjusted EPS of $0.38, both comfortably above consensus estimates of $15.1 billion and $0.27.

A Blowout Quarter

Intel delivered its strongest revenue growth in more than 15 years on Thursday, posting second-quarter 2026 results that crushed Wall Street expectations on nearly every metric. Revenue rose 25% year-over-year to $16.1 billion, well ahead of the $14.4 billion consensus. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.42, nearly double the $0.22 analysts had forecast. In the same quarter last year, Intel reported a loss of $0.10 per share on revenue of $12.9 billion.

https://x.com/intel/status/2080389994368098495

Shares jumped as much as 12% in after-hours trading, though the stock remains about 29% below its all-time closing high of $140.94 set on June 22 amid a broader rotation out of chip stocks.

"AI is driving unprecedented demand for compute, and as we continue to execute, Intel is well-positioned to capture sustainable growth across our CPU franchise, ASICs, advanced packaging and vast wafer foundry network."

— Lip-Bu Tan, Intel CEO

Data Centers and AI Leading the Charge

The standout performer was Intel's data center and AI segment, where revenue soared 59% to $6.3 billion — well above the $5.6 billion analysts anticipated. CFO Dave Zinsner told investors during the earnings call that Intel's AI-driven business grew more than 70% and now accounts for roughly 70% of the company's total revenue.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=fiZ_GWGcFY0

The surge reflects a fundamental shift in how AI is being deployed. As the industry moves from training large language models to running autonomous "agentic" AI systems — software agents that carry out tasks like coding, research, and customer service on behalf of users — demand for general-purpose CPUs has rebounded sharply alongside the GPU buildout that benefited rivals like Nvidia.

"In data centers, the CPU is taking off," Tan told Bloomberg. "Demand is outpacing our increasing supply, and so those are good problems to have."

Foundry Momentum and Big-Name Customers

Intel's foundry business, which manufactures chips for external customers, posted $5.77 billion in Q2 revenue, up 31% year-over-year and ahead of the $5.55 billion estimate. The segment is central to Intel's broader turnaround strategy under Tan, who took the CEO role in March 2025 with a mandate to rebuild the company's manufacturing credibility.

Two high-profile customer wins have bolstered that effort. Tesla has signed on as a customer for Intel's next-generation 14A manufacturing process for its "Terafab" AI chip project. Earlier this year, President Donald Trump announced that Apple had agreed to manufacture processors with Intel. Zinsner said the company has also secured long-term agreements with data center customers for CPUs and specialized chips called XPUs, some including both volume and price commitments.

Developments during Q2 prompted Intel to become "fully committed" to high-volume production using its 14A technology by 2028, Tan said.

Raising the Stakes on Spending

To meet surging demand, Intel raised its 2026 capital expenditure forecast from $18 billion to over $20 billion. Zinsner said the company is "meaningfully increasing" investments in equipment, clean room space, and substrates to support growth across both its product and foundry businesses.

Adjusted gross margins came in at 41.8%, above the 39% consensus forecast. However, under GAAP accounting, Intel reported an $11 billion net loss, reflecting the heavy cost of ramping new manufacturing processes and building out foundry capacity — expenses that weigh on reported results even as the operational business accelerates.

The Q3 outlook was equally bullish: Intel guided revenue of $15.8 billion to $16.8 billion and adjusted earnings of $0.38 per share, compared with analyst estimates of $15.1 billion and $0.27.

What It Means for Indian Tech Professionals

Intel's resurgence carries direct implications for the Indian diaspora. The company operates one of its largest global R&D centers in Bangalore and employs thousands of engineers across India. A growing capital budget and expanding product lines typically translate into increased hiring for engineering and design roles — opportunities relevant to both India-based professionals and Indian-Americans in Silicon Valley.

The broader AI infrastructure buildout also reinforces demand for semiconductor talent, an area where Indian engineers are heavily represented across the industry. Intel's foundry expansion, backed by U.S. government incentives under the CHIPS Act, aligns with India's own push to develop domestic semiconductor manufacturing capabilities.

What to Watch

Intel's stock has gained 172% year-to-date, but the recent 29% pullback from its June peak reflects broader investor anxiety about whether the pace of AI infrastructure spending is sustainable. The Q3 guidance suggests Intel sees no slowdown, but execution on the 14A manufacturing timeline and the foundry's ability to deliver for marquee clients like Apple and Tesla will be the true tests of whether this comeback has staying power.
